chapter_theme: The second part of இல்வாழ்க்கை, ten verses: a gift spoiled by withholding a sweet word, penance as an even mind not a sect's mark, prompt return of a deposit, the use of even a small companion, the bar on flesh for renouncers and for the graceless, service to the one who feeds one, bearing the anger of kin one has fed, and ingratitude as cutting one's own branch and burning the house one ate in.

338.reading: The verse says that to give clothing, medicine, shelter, food and the like and relieve a man's want, and then to send him off without a sweet word, is like killing a buffalo for a feast and being stingy over the spice.
338.nuance: The costly things are all given; what is withheld is the one thing that costs nothing, the word at parting (விடுத்து). The proverb's காயம் is the seasoning, cheap beside the slaughtered buffalo, so the meanness is measured by how little was saved.

pazhamozhi.literal: a man who has slaughtered a buffalo grudges the spice

story.act: no story; the proverb's feast-giver kills the buffalo and then stints on the seasoning

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a large gift spoiled by withholding a sweet word when the receiver is sent off

339.reading: The verse says that the marks each sect takes for itself are not penance, and that penance is the worth of one who keeps an even mind whether he is hacked or smeared with sandal paste and so lives on in the world, like the middle pin of a yoke.
339.nuance: The middle pin (பகலாணி) holds the yoke balanced between the two oxen, so the image is of a mind that leans to neither the wound nor the perfume. The verse sits under இல்வாழ்க்கை but its counsel is about penance; the heading does not fit it. செத்துக and சகத்தனாய் are odd forms, and the sense of line 2 is read from the pairing of cutting and sandal.

pazhamozhi.literal: like the middle pin of a yoke

story.act: no story; the yoke-pin stays at the centre whichever way the oxen pull

pazhamozhi.applied_to: true penance as an equal mind toward harm and honour, not the sect's outward mark

340.reading: The verse says that when someone has placed a thing in one's hand, one should hand it back at the moment he comes to take it, and not put him off thinking that he will not claim it and it has become one's settled wealth, for base wealth does not stay hidden.
340.nuance: The fault named is delay, not denial: the keeper need only stall (நீட்டித்தல்) for the deposit to begin turning into his own. புலை here qualifies wealth, the ill-kept thing, and is not a caste word.

pazhamozhi.literal: base wealth does not stay; it comes out into the open

story.act: no story; wrongly held wealth neither lasts nor stays concealed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: returning a deposit promptly when it is asked for

341.reading: The verse tells the man of the good land whose hills touch the sky that it is good to have a companion, since even a crab freed a brahmin from the danger of a snake, and that there is nothing which is of no use to something.
341.nuance: The point turns on நண்டேயும், 'even a crab': the companion need not be great to save one. பார்ப்பான் names the traveller in the tale and carries no rule. The heading இல்வாழ்க்கை fits only loosely.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is nothing that is of no use to something

story.act: a crab kept as a companion saved a brahmin from a snake

pazhamozhi.applied_to: having a companion, however small, against sudden danger

342.reading: The verse says that for those who have put away strong desire that is hard to let go and stood on the good path that is hard to walk, to eat flesh got through another's suffering is to swim across the sea and then drown in the water of a calf's hoofprint.
342.nuance: The sea is the craving already crossed; the hoofprint is a small appetite left over, so the ruin is the more absurd for the size of what was overcome. கற்றடி is read as the calf's hoofprint (கன்று அடி). The heading இல்வாழ்க்கை does not fit a verse addressed to renouncers.

norm.note: the abstention from flesh of the period, made a condition of the renouncer's path

pazhamozhi.literal: having swum the sea, to sink in a calf's hoofprint

story.act: no story; a swimmer crosses the ocean and drowns in a puddle

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the renouncer who has overcome great desire and then eats flesh

343.reading: The verse says that those who kill in rage and long rejoice in it, and do not walk in grace through understanding, do not refrain from killing other lives and living on their flesh, and that this is like spoiling the curd to cook something else.
343.nuance: The order runs from rage to killing to eating: flesh-eating is the last step of a habit that began without அருள். The proverb is read as giving up the good thing at hand (the curd, grace) to make some other dish; the image is not certain.

norm.note: the rule against killing and flesh of the period, grounded in grace

pazhamozhi.literal: to spoil the curd and cook something else

story.act: no story; the cook ruins the curd to make another dish

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those without grace who kill and eat flesh

344.reading: The verse tells the lord of the shore where waves roll that those who know a thing well should always plan the good of the one who gives them a measure of grain, and closes with the proverb that there is no trade in which one becomes two even by going over the sea.
344.nuance: The giver of a நாழி is the one who feeds the speaker, a patron or master. The proverb can be read two ways: that no trade, however far, doubles the capital as serving one's provider does, or that one gains nothing by seeking a richer master abroad. ஒன்றிண்டாம் is read as ஒன்றிரண்டாம்.
344.domain_note: a dependent toward the one who feeds him

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no trade in which one becomes two, even by crossing the water

story.act: no story; overseas trade does not double what is sent

pazhamozhi.applied_to: steady care for the welfare of the one who provides

345.reading: The verse says that one who gave two measures to a man as his own does not flare up even when that man rages at him like Yama, and asks who else but our own, scorning us as 'that one' and 'this one', would lick our ghee.
345.nuance: The giver bears the kinsman's anger because the gift made him one of his own; only kin take such liberty and still eat from the house. The line division and the subject of காயினும் are uncertain, and line 2 is corrupt.

pazhamozhi.literal: who else would lick our ghee?

story.act: no story; only one's own people take freely of the household's ghee

pazhamozhi.applied_to: bearing the rudeness of kin one has fed

346.reading: The verse tells the lord of the high hills of bright gems that to plot ruin with others against those who sought one out and cared for one well as their own is thoughtlessly to cut the branch on which one sits.

pazhamozhi.literal: to cut down the branch one was sitting on

story.act: no story; the sitter saws through his own perch

pazhamozhi.applied_to: plotting with others against one's benefactor

347.reading: The verse says that when someone has looked after a man and his kin as old friends and relieved their want, to join with those who have broken with him and speak against him behind his back is like setting fire to the house where one has eaten.

pazhamozhi.literal: like setting fire to the house where one ate

story.act: no story; the guest burns his host's house

pazhamozhi.applied_to: backbiting a benefactor in league with his enemies

links.note: Kural 92 ranks sweet speech above glad giving; Pazhamozhi 338 says a gift of food, clothes, medicine and shelter is spoiled if the sweet word is withheld at parting.
links.teaches: Read together, sweet speech is not only the higher of two separable goods but the finishing part of a gift, so its absence cheapens what was given.
links.list_adds: it names the costly gifts one by one and then the missing word, so the proverb measures the meanness by the gap between a slaughtered buffalo and the spice.

links.note: Elathi 7 counts sweet speech with mingling, a seat and good food in the host's gift; Pazhamozhi 338 isolates the word given at the guest's leaving.
links.teaches: Elathi joins the sweet word to food in one welcome, and Pazhamozhi shows the welcome can fail at its last moment, when the departing guest is dismissed without it.

links.note: Kural 280 says shaving or long hair are not needed if one gives up what the world blames; Pazhamozhi 339 also sets aside the sect's marks and says what penance is: an even mind under the blade and the sandal.
links.teaches: The Kural removes the outward marks by a negative test, and Pazhamozhi supplies a positive one, equanimity toward harm and honour, as the substance the marks pretend to.
links.list_adds: its yoke-pin proverb gives the inward test an image of balance the couplet lacks, centring penance on a mind pulled equally both ways.

links.note: The Siddhar song says forest, rags and begging bowl gain nothing without inner love; Pazhamozhi 339 says the sect's mark is not penance without an even mind.
links.teaches: Both deny that garb makes the ascetic, but they put different things in its place, love for the Lord in the Siddhar and Jain-style equanimity in Pazhamozhi.

links.note: Thirikadugam 62 names the man who wrongly keeps a deposit among three whose line is lost; Pazhamozhi 340 traces how keeping begins, by delaying the return in the hope that the owner will not claim it.
links.teaches: The pair shows the sin and its root: the Thirikadugam punishes the kept deposit, and Pazhamozhi locates the fault already in stalling when the owner asks.

links.note: Kural 283 says wealth got by stealth perishes even as it seems to grow; Pazhamozhi 340 applies the same doom to a deposit held back, saying base wealth does not stay.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi counts the withheld deposit as stealth without any taking, so the Kural's rule on stolen gain reaches a thing that came into one's hand lawfully.
links.list_adds: it moves the couplet's claim from theft to trust, the thing placed in one's hand, and adds the time of return as the test.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 63 says small gifts given without calling them of small use bear great fruit; Pazhamozhi 341 says nothing is of no use to something, since even a crab saved a man.
links.teaches: The two refuse the judgment 'too small to matter' from both sides, of the gift one gives and of the companion one keeps.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 136 says those cherished as a store against bad days fail one in trouble; Pazhamozhi 341 says even the smallest companion may save one.
links.teaches: Within one book help is shown to come from where it is not counted on, the crab, and to fail where it was banked on, the cherished friend.

links.note: Naladiyar 121 sets flesh-eaters among those who do not turn to renunciation; Pazhamozhi 342 says one who has renounced and then eats flesh undoes the whole crossing.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar makes flesh-eating a mark of the unrenounced, and Pazhamozhi adds that renunciation once achieved can still be sunk by it.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the sea and the hoofprint ranks the craving overcome against the small appetite kept, a contrast of scale the quatrain does not draw.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 342 addresses renouncers who eat flesh; 343 addresses those who kill in rage and lack grace.
links.teaches: The adjacent verses carry the bar on flesh from the renouncer's path to anyone without grace, and give it two roots: leftover appetite and anger.

links.note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh can hold to grace; Pazhamozhi 343 traces the flesh-eater back through killing to rage, and says he did not walk in grace.
links.teaches: The Kural states the incompatibility of flesh and grace, and Pazhamozhi gives its order in a life: anger first, then killing, then eating.
links.list_adds: its chain of rage, killing and eating sets the diet among its causes, and the curd proverb casts grace as the good thing spoiled.

links.note: Thirikadugam 36 names the flesh-eater who claims compassion; Pazhamozhi 343 says those who eat flesh do not walk in grace.
links.teaches: Both deny the meat-eater's claim to grace, one by exposing his self-serving reasoning and the other by tracing the habit back to anger.

links.note: Kural 104 says those who know the fruit take a millet's good as a palm; Pazhamozhi 344 asks the knowing to plan always for the good of one who gives them a measure of grain.
links.teaches: The Kural enlarges a small kindness in the mind, and Pazhamozhi turns that into lasting service toward a provider, framed as a return no trade can match.
links.list_adds: it moves the couplet from a single favour to a standing tie of maintenance, and its trade proverb puts gratitude in the language of profit.

links.note: Naladiyar 357 says the worthy bear many faults from one who did them a kindness; Pazhamozhi 345 has the giver bear the anger of the kinsman he fed.
links.teaches: The pair runs patience both ways along a gift: the receiver bears the benefactor's faults in the Naladiyar, and the giver bears the receiver's rage in Pazhamozhi.
links.list_adds: it reverses the quatrain's direction and grounds the forbearance in kinship made by giving, with the ghee proverb as its sign.

links.note: Kural 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, aram plots the plotter's; Pazhamozhi 346 says plotting against one's benefactor is cutting the branch one sits on.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves the return to aram, while Pazhamozhi needs no agent: the benefactor is the plotter's own support, so the ruin is self-inflicted at once.
links.list_adds: it narrows the couplet to the one who cared for the plotter and joins others to the plot, and its proverb makes the retribution mechanical.

links.note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; Pazhamozhi 347 names one form of it, joining the benefactor's enemies and backbiting him.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks ingratitude as beyond remedy, and Pazhamozhi gives it a concrete shape in speech and alliance, likened to burning the house that fed one.
links.list_adds: it specifies the ingrate's act as backbiting in company with the estranged and weighs it by the past meals, which the couplet does not name.

links.note: Both close the heading with ingratitude; 346 is plotting ruin, 347 is backbiting in league with enemies.
links.teaches: The two proverbs split ingratitude's harm: cutting one's own branch ruins the traitor, burning the house one ate in ruins the benefactor.

source_issues: 339: செத்துக and சகத்தனாய் (line 2-3) are odd forms; the line is read as 'whether hacked or smeared with sandal'.
341: விண்டோ யும் (line 2) has a stray space, read as விண்தோயும்.
344: ஒன்றிண்டாம் in the proverb is read as ஒன்றிரண்டாம்.
345: தான்காயான மன்னே (line 2) looks corrupt; the opening quotation mark falls inside மற்றியாரே, so the proverb as printed begins with றியாரே.
